title: The Black Hole At The Center Of Biden’s Education Plan
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler observes that President Biden's education plan funds preschool and community college but says almost nothing about the years between ages five and eighteen. She argues this gap matters because U.S. reading and achievement results are weak and efforts at either end will be undermined by what happens in elementary school. Preschool gains fade out and most community college entrants land in remedial courses. Using E.D. Hirsch's account of France, where a shift from a knowledge-based national curriculum to skills in 1989 widened the gap between rich and poor, she contends that the missing ingredient is a coherent, content-rich elementary curriculum. She urges federal leaders to at least name that cause and point to Louisiana's content-focused approach, and suggests that dropping meaningless skills practice would make twelve years enough.
points: A plan that funds preschool and college but skips K-12 ignores the stage where knowledge and vocabulary gaps are actually built or left unaddressed.
Preschool gains typically fade by third grade, and most community college students need non-credit remedial work, so the ends of the pipeline cannot compensate for elementary schools.
France's 1989 shift from a prescribed, sequenced curriculum to a skills emphasis produced decline and a widening gap by background, a cautionary parallel for the U.S.
Heavy practice of comprehension skills such as finding the main idea crowds out social studies, science and the arts that build the knowledge reading depends on.
Wexler points to Louisiana's content-focused ELA curriculum and aligned reading tests as a model that federal policy could encourage.
quotes: Efforts to improve education before kindergarten and after 12th grade will be largely undermined by what is happening—or not happening—in between. Yes, we’ve tried many things, but not the one thing science tells us can work—namely, building children’s academic knowledge and vocabulary through a coherent curriculum at the elementary level.

Evidence on the effects of preschool in the U.S. is decidedly mixed. Children often start kindergarten with an advantage, but by third grade it generally disappears, a phenomenon known as preschool fadeout.

But in 1989, the government declared that French elementary schools would no longer follow the prescribed state curriculum, which had continued to introduce substantive knowledge in a logical sequence. Instead, each school would decide its own focus, and “the emphasis was to be on skills, not facts.” The result was an overall decline in performance and a growing gap between rich and poor, even though nothing else in the system had changed.

That’s essentially what American elementary schools have been doing as well, especially over the last twenty years. The high-stakes reading and math tests ushered in by No Child Left Behind have only exacerbated an already heavy focus on reading comprehension “skills” like “finding the main idea,” which are practiced for hours every week while potentially knowledge-building subjects like social studies, science, and the arts fall by the wayside.

Like preschool, free community college could be a good investment, but in the U.S. more than two-thirds of enrolling students are required to take remedial math or English classes that don’t earn credit. Most never graduate, and fewer than 25% of all students at two-year colleges complete a degree within three years.
Using the power of the federal government to improve education is tricky. In the U.S., curriculum and instruction are traditionally matters of local control, and that’s where change needs to come.

But if the rest of the world is doing a much better job with those twelve years, four additional years is unlikely to make a difference. And if we stop wasting so many precious hours on largely meaningless “skills” in elementary school and beyond, we may find that twelve years is plenty of time to equip students for jobs that enable both them and the United States to thrive.
